title: Ang 1157–1162: Kabir in Bhairao
tomorrow: what happens when a child begs God to drink his milk?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 1136: Guru Arjan set aside the fasts and pilgrimages of both neighbors, and two readings met in one line. Serve the One. Now the Gurus' voices end, and a weaver's begins.

Money now is mostly a number on a screen. You can't feel it in your hand or hear it clink. For a long time, in a lot of places, you kept it tied in a knot in the corner of a cloth: a scarf, a turban end, a dupatta. You could feel it against you all day, a little hard lump that said you're safe. On ang 1157 the weaver Kabir picks up that knot and refuses to tie it.
screen: `MONEY YOU CAN'T FEEL.` → `COINS IN THE CORNER OF A CLOTH.` → `KABIR WON'T TIE THE KNOT.`

segments.voice: Here the Gurus' Bhairao hymns end and the Bhagats begin, the saint-poets whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth. First comes Kabir, remembered as a weaver. In paraphrase, his hymn opens: this wealth of mine is the Lord's Name. I don't tie it in a knot. I don't sell it to buy my food. Feel the two things he's turning down. The knot is guarding: wealth you clutch, check, worry about. Selling is spending: wealth you trade away for something else. Ordinary money is always one or the other, saved or spent. Kabir says the Name, Naam, is neither. You can't lock it up, and you can't cash it out. It isn't less real for that; the hymn calls it his wealth, his capital. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Granth puts a weaver's hymns right beside the Gurus' own, in the same raga, after the same morning hymns, as scripture. Notice too what Kabir doesn't say. He doesn't say money is evil, or that you shouldn't save. He's talking about a different kind of wealth, the kind you can't feel against your hip, and saying it's the one he trusts. Kabir: the knot left untied.
screen: `THE BHAGATS BEGIN: KABIR.` · `THIS WEALTH IS THE NAME.` · `NOT KNOTTED, NOT SOLD.` · `A WEAVER BESIDE THE GURUS.` · then, large: `KABIR.`

segments.voice: Find a string, a shoelace, or the corner of a scarf, and tie a firm knot in it. Hold it, feel how tight it is. Then slowly untie it, lay it down, and sit for the rest of the time with your hand open on your knee. If you'd like, read ang 1158 before you begin.
Ang 1157. Where Kabir's Bhairao hymns begin, and the weaver calls the Name a wealth he won't knot up or sell.
Kabir: a weaver who left the knot untied. Some wealth you can only keep by not clutching it. That's today.

chat.says: a kid keeps his camp tokens knotted in his sock "so nobody gets them." how do i explain Kabir's line?
options: tokens are fine in a sock. Kabir's line is about the Name: wealth you can't knot up.
tell him Kabir says hidden wealth is the safest, so the sock is smart.

chat.meaning: Kabir calls the Name a wealth he won't knot up or sell. He's not judging tokens or savings; he's naming a different kind of wealth.

Kabir.meaning: a saint-poet, remembered as a weaver; his hymns are in the Granth

dupatta.meaning: a long scarf worn with Punjabi dress
